analysis.one_liner: Lets college athletes cash in on their fame, while declaring them non-employees and shielding NCAA rules from antitrust suits.
analysis.headline: Both House committees approved the bill (final committee vote 30-23) and a rule for floor debate was filed December 1, 2025; the House has not voted yet.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill writes into federal law that college athletes may sign name, image, and likeness (NIL) endorsement deals and hire agents, and it requires athletic departments with $20 million or more in annual revenue to cover athletes' sports injuries for three years after they leave school, keep scholarships through injury, help former athletes finish degrees, and field at least 16 varsity teams. In exchange, it states that no athlete can ever be considered an employee, protects NCAA rules from antitrust lawsuits, and wipes out state laws that regulate athlete pay, employment status, or eligibility. It also requires colleges to disclose how much of students' tuition fees subsidize athletics, and bans student fees from funding athletics at schools taking in $50 million or more a year in media rights money.
analysis.who_benefits: College athletes gain enforceable NIL rights, guaranteed medical care for sports injuries (including three years after graduation), scholarships that can't be pulled for injury, degree-completion aid, protections against agent overcharging, and disclosure of how their schools spend student fees. The NCAA and major conferences also gain heavily: new federal authority to write the rules on eligibility, transfers, and recruiting, an antitrust shield, and a permanent bar on athletes claiming employee status.

how_it_helps.text: No school, conference, or the NCAA may restrict an athlete's ability to sign an NIL deal or hire an agent.

Athletic departments with $20 million or more in annual revenue must pay for medical care for sports injuries through enrollment and at least three years after graduation, provide mental health services, maintain scholarships regardless of injury or performance, and fund degree-completion aid for former athletes.
Those same institutions must maintain at least 16 varsity sports teams, and the reported version requires Title IX compliance in doing so, preserving opportunities in women's and Olympic sports.
Sports agents cannot charge more than 5% on endorsement contracts, agreements over $600 must be in writing with termination rights, and state attorneys general can enforce violations.

Colleges must publicly report how much student fee money supports athletics, and schools with $50 million or more in annual media rights revenue are barred from using student fees for their athletic programs.
Athletes get at least one transfer with immediate eligibility, and schools must tell transferring athletes which of their credits will count.

analysis.who_pays: Big-revenue athletic departments bear new costs for injury coverage, mental health services, and degree-completion programs. Agents face fee caps and disclosure duties. The largest cost falls on athletes themselves, who permanently give up employee status, antitrust claims, and stronger state-law protections. Non-athlete students gain from fee transparency but the bill leaves ordinary athletic fees in place at all but the richest schools.

drawbacks.text: The bill states that no athlete may be considered an employee of a school, conference, or the NCAA under any federal or state law, foreclosing unionization, workers' compensation, and wage claims.
Any rule the NCAA adopts under the bill is declared lawful under federal and state antitrust laws, stripping athletes of the antitrust suits that produced earlier wins like the House settlement.
The bill preempts state laws governing athlete compensation, benefits, employment status, and eligibility, overriding stronger state protections.
Schools may only pay athletes up to a 'pool limit' set at 22% of the average sports revenue of the 70 highest-earning members, capping total direct compensation at the richest programs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Athletes at big-revenue schools get genuine, concrete gains: injury coverage, protected scholarships, degree completion, and enforceable NIL rights. But the price is the permanent loss of the two levers — employee status and antitrust lawsuits — that courts and state legislatures had been using to win those very gains, and a federal cap on how much schools can pay. The bargain favors athletes only if the NCAA delivers on the benefit commitments now that its legal exposure is gone; the bill includes reporting requirements but few enforcement teeth beyond state attorneys general.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared two House committees in September and the Rules Committee filed a rule on December 1 setting up floor debate, but the House has not voted and Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced July 10, 2025, by Rep. Gus Bilirakis with both Republican and Democratic original cosponsors.
A subcommittee forwarded it by a vote of 12-11 on July 15, and on July 23 the full committee ordered it reported by votes of 18-17 and 30-23.
Both the Energy and Commerce and Education and Workforce Committees reported the bill on September 11, 2025, and it was placed on the Union Calendar.
On December 1, 2025, the Rules Committee reported a resolution providing for House consideration of the bill under a closed rule, which allows only limited amendments from the floor.
The reported version was amended to include a Title IX savings clause and Title IX compliance requirements for the 16-sport minimum.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No final outcome yet: the bill's backers have moved it to the brink of House floor consideration, while opponents' concerns remain unaddressed and unresolved.

sides.party_line_note: Committee votes were razor-thin — 12-11, 18-17, and 30-23 — while sponsorship was bipartisan (15 of 223 Republicans and 7 of 217 Democrats), so the bill advanced mainly on Republican votes with a small bipartisan core.

industries.industry: NCAA and major college sports programs
industries.note: The bill locks in the NCAA's role as rulemaker for college sports, grants its rules antitrust immunity, and permanently bars athletes from employee status — while also imposing real benefit obligations on big-revenue schools. Its legal gains come directly at the cost of athletes' potential wage and antitrust claims.

The bill defines school-affiliated collectives as 'associated entities' and bars most direct payments from them to athletes, and caps total school-paid compensation under a revenue-based pool limit. This curbs recruiting inducements but also cuts off a payment stream athletes had been using.

Agents face a 5% fee cap on endorsement contracts, mandatory disclosures, and voidable agreements lacking required terms, but gain a clearer legal framework and guaranteed athlete termination rights after enrollment ends.

The bill's preemption bars states from requiring releases of athletes' broadcast rights, stabilizing media companies' access to game footage, while the fee rules are keyed to schools' media rights revenue.

analysis.trajectory: With a closed rule already reported, House floor passage looks likely on mostly Republican votes. The Senate has shown no action on a companion, and bills of this kind have historically stalled there, so the realistic best case for supporters is House passage followed by a hard fight or quiet death in the Senate.
